1.s: “How the city sits solitary, that was full of people!” Jerusalem, pictured as a widow, weeps at night with no one to comfort her.
1.d: Each of its 22 three-line stanzas begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. Verse 3 echoes Moses’ warning in Deuteronomy 28:64–65 that disobedience would scatter the people [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]], and the city confesses that God was right (1:18) [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].

2.s: The Lord in his anger has destroyed Zion like an enemy; children faint in the streets. “Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord.”
2.d: This poem stresses God’s anger: he himself destroyed Jerusalem [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]] [[tosn:Lamentations 2:1–22]]. The blame falls on the false prophets who failed to warn the people (2:14) [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. It is an acrostic, with two letters in a different order [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].

3.s: A man who has seen affliction describes God’s hand against him, then turns: “his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.”
3.d: A triple acrostic: every line of each stanza starts with the same letter [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. The writer speaks of Judah’s suffering as his own [[tosn:Lamentations 3:1–24]]. Just as God was faithful in judging, he will be faithful in restoring those who return; his mercies are new each day [[tosn:Lamentations 3:22–33]] [[tosn:Lamentations 3:23]].

4.s: The gold has grown dim: the starvation and suffering of the siege, blamed on the sins of prophets and priests.
4.d: An acrostic of two-line stanzas [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. Judah believed Jerusalem could not fall, since God had saved it from Sennacherib [[tosn:Lamentations 4:12]]. “The anointed of Yahweh” who was captured is King Zedekiah [[tosn:Lamentations 4:20]] [[bible:2 Kings 25:4-7]].

5.s: A communal prayer: “Remember, Yahweh, what has come on us.” “Turn us to yourself, Yahweh, and we will be turned.”
5.d: Not an acrostic, but it has 22 verses, as many as the letters of the Hebrew alphabet [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. Its form shows the people’s confusion [[bsn:Lamentations 3:1–5:22]]. God answered its closing question through the prophets and by sending Christ [[tosn:Lamentations 5:22]].
